cards.prompt: **Drag the slider** until a computer would need **100+ years** to guess this password.
cards.explanation: A computer can make about a **billion guesses a second**. Each extra letter multiplies what it has to try by **26**, so 6 letters fall in under a second, but 14 would take thousands of years. **Length** is what makes a password strong.
cards.hint: Drag the slider to the right and watch the time shoot up.
cards.nudge: Keep going: every extra letter multiplies the time by 26.

cards.prompt: Which password would take a computer **longer** to guess?

options.nudge: Numbers and symbols help a little, but it's only 8 characters. Think back to the slider.
A word plus a year is one of the first things guessed, and it's still fairly short.

cards.hint: What made the time shoot up on the slider?
cards.explanation: **Length wins.** Four random words make a long password that's still easy to remember: a **passphrase**. Short ones with symbols, or a word plus a year, are guessed far sooner.

cards.title: Length wins
cards.body:
Adding capitals, numbers and symbols helps a little. **Length** helps a lot more.

The easiest length to remember is a **passphrase**: **four or more random words**, at least **15 characters**, like `violet cactus harbour pepper`. That's what Australia's cyber security experts at cyber.gov.au recommend.

The words must be **random**. Song lyrics, famous quotes and pet names are easy to guess.

cards.prompt:
Guessing computers don't start at `aaaa`. They try **common passwords** first, like `password123` and `qwerty`, then names, birthdays and swaps like `@` for `a`. (`password123` falls faster than you can say "password123".)

Is each password **easy to guess** or **hard to guess**?

items.label: Your pet's name and birth year
A long random mix of 16 characters

cards.explanation: Common passwords, keyboard patterns, names, birthdays and swaps like `@` for `a` are the **first things guessed**. Several random words, or a long random mix of characters, have to be found by trying every combination.
cards.hint: Think about what guessers try first: common passwords, patterns, names and birthdays, and swaps like @ for a.
cards.nudge: Swapping letters for symbols (`@`, `0`) doesn't fool a guessing computer. It tries those swaps early on.

cards.prompt: Now the password can be **10 characters at most**. Reach **100 years** anyway, by choosing which kinds of characters it can use.
cards.explanation: Mixing in capitals, numbers and symbols means more characters to choose from, so a **short random** password can reach 100 years too. But it's hard to remember. That's why long passphrases, or a password manager, work better for people.
cards.hint: At 10 characters, lowercase alone isn't enough. Turn on more kinds of characters and watch how many there are to choose from.
cards.nudge: Push the length to 10, then add kinds of characters until the time passes 100 years.

cards.prompt: Which of these makes the **best** passphrase?

options.nudge: Song lyrics and famous lines are in guessing lists. The words need to be random, not ones that belong together.
Pet names and birth years are easy for someone to find out or guess. Look for words with no link to you or to each other.
Swapping letters for symbols is one of the first tricks a guesser tries, and it's short. Look for length made of random words.

cards.explanation: Four **random, unrelated** words give length that's easy to remember and hard to guess. Lyrics, personal details and symbol swaps are all tried early by guessing computers.
cards.hint: Look for four or more words that have nothing to do with each other, or with you.

cards.prompt: Your friend Mia is proud of her new passphrase. It's a line from her favourite song: five words, 26 characters.

choices.text: Not really: song lines are in guessing lists, however long they are
choices.consequence: Right. Guessers try lyrics, quotes and famous lines early. Length only helps when the words are random.

choices.text: Yes: it's over 15 characters, so it's long enough to be strong
choices.consequence: Length isn't enough on its own. A famous line is in guessing lists, so it falls early.

choices.text: Yes, as long as she adds a symbol like ! to the very end
choices.consequence: A symbol on the end is one of the first tricks guessers try. The words themselves need to be random.

steps.text: Mia asks what she should do instead.

choices.text: Pick four or more random words that don't belong together
choices.consequence: Now it's long **and** unpredictable. She can still picture the words to remember them.

choices.text: Pick a line from an old song hardly anyone knows
choices.consequence: Guessing lists hold huge numbers of songs, not just popular ones. The words need to be random.

cards.explanation: A passphrase needs **random** words. Lyrics, quotes and sayings are long but predictable, so guessing computers try them early.
cards.hint: Think back to what makes a passphrase strong: length, and one more thing about the words.

cards.prompt:
Websites sometimes get hacked and their passwords stolen. That's a [[data breach]]. Attackers then try the stolen email and password on **other** websites.

Today a game website emails you: it was hacked, and passwords were stolen.

steps.text: You used the **same password** for that game and for your email. Your email can reset all your other passwords. What do you do first?

choices.text: Change your email password to a new, unique one
choices.consequence: Good. Your email is the most important account: it can reset all the others.

choices.text: Nothing. It's only a game account
choices.consequence: The same password opens your email too. Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites.
The stolen password still opens your email. That's the one to change first.

steps.text: Your email is safe again. What about the game account?

choices.text: Give it its own new password too
choices.consequence: Now each account has its own password, so one leak can't open the other.

choices.text: Use your new email password for the game as well
choices.consequence: Then the next breach could open your email again. Every account needs its own password.

cards.explanation: One stolen password shouldn't open two accounts. Change it everywhere you used it, starting with your **email**, which can reset everything else, and give every account its own password.
cards.hint: Think about which account could be used to reset all your others. Then think about why every account needs its own password.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Guessers try **common passwords**, names and patterns first.
- **Length** wins: a **passphrase** is four or more **random** words.
- Give every account its **own** password.

Next: a second lock on the door.
